newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia to raise arabica coffee output - report.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia to raise arabica coffee output - report.

text.p: Indonesia, the world's top robusta coffee producer, is making efforts to boost its production of the more expensive arabica variety, a country report presented at a regional meeting said on Thursday.

"The potential for improved arabica production is one of the brighter spots in Indonesian coffee production," said the report presented at the Asia-Pacific Consulative Forum on Coffee held on the tropical resort island of Bali.

The one-day, closed-door session was attended by delegates from from coffee producing countries such as the Philippines, Thailand and host Indonesia, the world's third largest coffee producer after Brazil and Colombia.
The meeting, held under the aegis of the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP), follows a three-day gathering of the International Coffee Organization (ICO).
The report said Indonesian efforts to boost arabica coffee output would be achieved by intensifying husbandry as well as converting highland robusta to arabica.

"In several areas, robusta is grown at highland areas which are more suitable and profitable for growing arabica coffee," the report said, adding that arabica was being grown in areas such as South Sulawesi, Aceh in North Sumatra and on Java.
The report did not give projections on arabica production, but said Indonesia had been forecast to produce 7.5 million 60-kg bags of coffee in 1996, including 450,000 bags of arabica.
It said Indonesia's domestic consumption of coffee would continue to grow, in line with its buoyant economic growth and rising standard of living.

It said the per capita consumption of coffee in Indonesia, the world's fourth most populous country with some 200 million people, was low at 0.5 kgs (one lb), compared with 2.9 kgs (6.4 lbs) in Japan and 2.2 kgs (4.9 lbs) in Australia and New Zealand.
The report also said the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters was considering setting up a coffee research institute.

"The institute will supply information regarding coffee cultivation, its botany and explore the aroma, flavour and body of brews of several collections of famous speciality coffee, both arabica and robusta from Indonesia," it said.
